record.paper_title: Nuclei of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs - Central engine & conditions of star formation: Workshop summary and open questions
record.context_brief: nature of G2/DSO near the Galactic Center
record.original_question: What is the physical nature of the G2/DSO source that was approaching the Galactic Center in 2013–2014: is it primarily a gas-and-dust cloud, a dust-enshrouded star, or something else, and how can near-infrared integral-field observations discriminate among the proposed scenarios?

evidence.quote: Current results on the closest galactic nucleus, the Galactic Center (GC), were presented, in particular the potential gas/dust cloud currently (2013-2014) approaching the GC. The nature of this source is still controvertial.

M. Schartmann described two possible scenarios for the evolution of the G2/DSO object based on hydrodynamical simulations. He also showed how NIR IFU observations of the evolution of the source can help in discriminating between these possible explanations.
A. Eckart, in turn, showed the first K-band identifications of G2/DSO, indicating that it might be a dust-enshrouded star in contrast to a pure gas and dust object.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Near the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A* at the Galactic Center, an infrared-excess source known as G2 (also called the Dusty S-cluster Object, DSO) was observed approaching pericenter on a highly eccentric orbit during 2013–2014. Two principal physical scenarios have been proposed for its nature: (i) a coreless, diffuse cloud composed of gas and dust, which would be tidally stretched and largely disrupted during pericenter passage; or (ii) a compact, dust-enshrouded star whose stellar core would survive pericenter passage, with only its outer envelope being significantly affected.

Determine which scenario correctly describes the physical nature of G2/DSO. In particular:

(a) Establish whether the source is primarily a pure gas-and-dust cloud, a dust-enshrouded (possibly young, accreting) star, or some other configuration.

(b) Specify the observational signatures—obtainable from near-infrared integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy and imaging (e.g., compactness versus tidal elongation of the Brγ recombination line emission, K- and L-band continuum identification, evolution of line-of-sight velocity and position across pericenter, and intrinsic polarization)—that discriminate between the cloud and dust-enshrouded-star scenarios.

(c) Predict the post-pericenter behavior (compactness, luminosity, and spectroscopic appearance) implied by each scenario and compare with observations.
artifact.status_search_result: Post-2014 near-infrared observations show that G2/DSO remained compact through pericenter (no tidal disruption into a stretched cloud), exhibits intrinsic polarization >20% and a strong Ks–L' excess, and behaves consistently with a dust-enshrouded young stellar object in an accretion phase rather than a pure gas-and-dust cloud. This interpretation has been extended to a class of similar G-objects near Sgr A*. The dust-enshrouded-star scenario is now broadly favored, though detailed properties (mass, age, accretion state) remain under investigation.

status_evidence.title: Polarized near-infrared light of the Dusty S-cluster Object (DSO/G2) at the Galactic Center
status_evidence.snippet: DSO/G2 is intrinsically polarized (>20%) and remains compact near pericenter, consistent with a dust-enshrouded young accreting star.
status_evidence.claim: Observations support the dust-enshrouded star interpretation over a pure cloud.

status_evidence.title: Galactic center G objects as dust-enshrouded stars near the supermassive black hole
status_evidence.snippet: G objects including G2/DSO are interpreted as dust-enshrouded stars near Sgr A*.
status_evidence.claim: The dust-enshrouded-star scenario has been extended to a population of similar objects.

status_evidence.title: Infrared-excess Source DSO/G2 Near the Galactic Center: Theory vs. Observations
status_evidence.snippet: Compact single-peak Brγ emission near pericenter disfavors the coreless-cloud hypothesis.
status_evidence.claim: Compactness through pericenter discriminates against the pure cloud scenario.
